item.title: Emergent Ego (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Sci-Fi / Esoteric

Elevator Pitch: Exposure to particular combinations of SCP files, or the knowledge therein, results in the emergence of deviant archetypal personalities with anomalous properties, which override the ego of the subject viewing the files; read certain SCP files, and become possessed by some unknown personality.

Central Narrative: Discovered when a Class-B staff member experienced a psychological break accompanied by anomalous change in personality, physiology, and working esoteric knowledge; review of foundation records revealed a similar incident in the past.

The only known commonality between the incidents is the exposure to a particular set of case files over a period of six months. These files, known in combination as [SCP Number]-1, represent one of possibly numerous patterns that cause archetypal emergence.

In the case of [SCP Number]-1, the emergence of the accompanying personality was retroactively associated with a number of symptoms prior to complete ego eclipse. These all occur prior to the full emergence of the archetypical personality. A psychological profile of the emergent personality is nonetheless included based on the data available.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Research ongoing: one D-Class personnel is to be exposed to the pattern of SCP files to try and replicate an emergence event. In addition, Foundation researchers, aided by onsite supercomputers, are parsing incident reports for similar commonalities to indicate additional patterns and corresponding archetypes.

Additional Notes: This SCP is meant to serve a dual purpose, as a frame story for an SCP podcast that I'm working on — I want to be up front that this is ultimately my intention, but I still fully believe that the idea can stand alone as an entry, and in no way am I trying to create a subpar SCP just to enable a related venture. My primary goal is to make this SCP happen, and, should it be approved and see some success, I'll then explore additional creative avenues with it.

The podcast will be from the perspective of the D-Class personnel being exposed to articles (under the pretense of reading and recording them for accessibility use within the Foundation). The D-Class in question will slowly deteriorate into this emergent personality over the course of the podcast, as a part of the overarching narrative.

item.title: Seeking Greenlight- The Book of Omens
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Green light: Yes
Page Type: SCP article
Elevator Pitch:A photo album that can predict disasters and death.
Central Narrative: A long explanation of how the photo album works. It shows photos of a woman in various places, from various time periods. Depending on how long the viewer has to live, the woman will appear to be a different age. The places she appears in the photos are sites of famous disasters shortly before they happened, such as 9/11 or Chernobyl. The article ends with the writer speculating they could use the book to predict containment breaches or disasterous experiments by having their personnel look at the book, but then there's an addendum. A new photo has appeared in the book, and the background is the SCP site it's being held in.
Hook: Through the course of the story, the book seems relatively harmless (if a little disturbing) but some things, like the name of the site it's held at, are redacted for unclear reasons. Then at the end, why it was redacted becomes clear, and it raises whole new questions about the true nature of the book and the future.
Additional notes: This might be more a question for full draft editing, but I'm not sure whether to spice it up with more speculations or hints about how dangerous the book actually is, or whether to keep it more passive or mysterious. (Adding notes from one researcher to another, test logs, etc.)

item.title: It Will Not Leave
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror, Drama/Emotional

Page Layout (Optional): Interviews and incident logs to be included.

Elevator Pitch: : An MTF officer starts to spot in random situations a former squad companion who died in an earlier Containment operation. Despite Foundation help with amnestics, the visions become more frequent and intense.

Central Narrative: Adam and Samuel have been friends since nursery times: they attended the same high school and joined the police academy at the same time. After some time in a police station, they are recruited by the SCP Foundation to join a MTF. Some years later, during a Containment operation, Samuel fails to follow protocol and ends up with Adam dead. The grief and sense of guilt pursuits Samuel to the point that starts to see Adam during his routine more often with time, to the point that jeopardizes other companions during some MTF operations. After a psychological test, he is given an amnestic to forget about his friend and stick to the MTF. However, after some time without issues, during an intense MTF operation, Samuel provokes a containment breach as he claims that an unknown individual appeared to him. This appearance will never leave from then on. After providing a description to the psychologist, matching that of Adam, he is given another amnestic. The entity does not disappear though, and it starts to directly intervene in Adam’s actions, deterring him from any basic activity. Foundation demotes him and keeps him a study subject, classifying Adam’s apparition as an SCP object. Eventually, Samuel commits suicide. An MTF operative from Samuel’s former MTF squad is recorded in a tapped phone call claiming that he has spotted Samuel in his garden and is afraid of reporting this to the Foundation.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Adam’s apparition to Samuel is not real. It is driven by strong feelings of guilt, grief and melancholy. The abnormality comes from the exaggerated expression of these feelings, which get so stuck to Samuel and his subconscious that even amnestics cannot fully support Samuel. In benefit of maintaining resources, rather than promoting an adequate mental health, Foundation classifies it as an anomaly and moves on. Samuel’s sorrow becomes a memetic effect.

Additional Notes: There are two main ideas that I wanted to explore. First, how even long-term friendship can deeply mark an individual; and second, the HRM policy of the Foundation regarding its MTF operatives, and the perils of mental health mismanagement.

item.title: Re: SCP Idea - A house and its occupant
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

will be told from a first person perspective of XXXX-A

This line here, and the central narrative section as a whole, raises one question to me: why isn't this a tale? Like it absolutely could work as a SCP! But the focus here feels very much on the woman and what she wants and how she feels about everything, and to me, that's often best written as a tale where you can really like…just get in her head in a way you can't with diary entries and interviews.

Beyond this, my biggest concern is you have this really nice setting for a story, where you have all these elements and ways to get them into play, but you don't really do much with them: once she's in containment, not much really happens and it feels like this is just…really calling out for more conflict and the story to like… go somewhere, y'know?

Like, you mention:

in return, she performs tests with the Foundation

But it's not clear either what these tests are or how they're tying into the narrative here and at the end of the day, this feels…almost like a slice of life piece but where there's only really one character and I'm not sure there's enough meat here to get away with it?

item.title: Re: Amateur wizards and how to contain them
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

A modern day architect can’t explain exactly how the great pyramids were built, but can gain a basic understanding by examining them, and probably come up with a Rough theory. This scp can do the same with magical/ mythical items.

So like…is the anomaly here 'the SCP has anomalous knowledge'? Cos this just feels like the SCP is effectively a reality bender and so like…not necessarily something particularly of interest here? Like even to the Foundation, it feels like if they can't control him, they could literally just find a different reality bender, y'know?

My biggest concern with this is that the narrative feels…very passive? There's not a lot driving it forwards since the SCP just kinda gets better at doing magic stuff and the Foundation respond by locking them up more and it feels like it really needs to be tied into the whole angle of the foundation utilising it more: like, to really explore the interplay between 'we keep showing him new magic so we can figure out what's happening' and 'every time we do this, he learns how to do this'; with like…the Foundation openly considering ways around this like 'what if we amnesticise him'.

It also feels like it doesn't really end up going somewhere: it keeps escalating until it reaches a point where it just kinda…stops without there being any kinda…big event or real sense of closure.

item.title: Re: The Three Sided Coin
item.content:encoded:
noting that since there's a lot of stuff in the thread, I haven't read it all. I'm assuming the main post covers all the important details and apologies if I miss stuff as a result

[+] Open for crit
– hide block

The coins most interesting part isn't the monster but more so what it does to the people in possession of it. It makes them more exuberant, more fond of games and gambling, risk, chaos, but not necessarily evil.

My concern here is that it feels a little too much like the coin is forcing this to happen; whereas a story like this often works best when the coin has some kinda property that gently encourages it and leads to people choosing to become this way. Like, imagine if the coin was anomalously lucky say, and caused people who gamble with it to win a bit more often than usual: not enough to be immediately obvious but enough to be beneficial; and in turn, this sense of always being able to win causes them to take more and more risks because they think it'll pay off and then eventually it doesn't, y'know?

This ties into a concern I have here: the monster feels irrelevant. Like, this has three faces, so presumably (though there's no indication of this) it has a 1-in-3 chance of landing monster side up; which in turn means they are very likely to have turned into a monster within 3 flips.

Beyond this my largest concern is: what story(s) are you actually telling here? Like you talk a lot about how this concept can be used to create stories and the general of like, how it affects someone who uses it but really what I want to know is the specific: what arc are you telling here? What are you putting in the SCP article and the tales?

item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit

Do you think any interviews (mayhaps just one, and a test involving the interviewed, like the family I suggested above) would be beneficial, or do you suggest I focus the entire rest of my writing on the creator of the phenomenon, and his goals?

It really depends on how you structure this. An interview with someone affected by this could be a really good way to put a human face on the consequences of what the creator has done; and indeed, you could have a series of interviews through this where you have like, a section covering something the creator has done to make it better followed by like, the interview showing what the broader consequences of this are say.

Interviews with the creator could also be a great way to explore like,,,why he did this and what he was trying to achieve.

Equally, they could feel completely extraneous and unnecessary here and it really depends on what you want the focus to be?

How do these ideas sound to you? In what way should I reformat my ideas further to fit the mold of an acceptable article?

At the moment, it feels like this just needs a little time to consider the full arc here: like, we have the beginning of the story where the creator makes the SCP, and then….where does it go? The idea of it being an unsettling mistake is good; and leads to the idea that maybe the creator tries to fix it; and then…I just want to see where all that goes, y'know?

item.title: Re: The Serpent
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

This feels like an anomaly with a big grab bag of anomalous abilities and I really urge you to like, strip it down to just a single (or a few linked) abilities, over a thing with a big list of cool things it can do. A more complex SCP doesn't become more interesting; and adding anomalous properties to explain why the Foundation can't just do [thing] is a bad reason to add them.

Beyond this: the central narrative section feels very, passive? It comes across more like a series of events than as a coherent story, since there's not a lot driving the Foundation's research forwards; and the ending feels very…contrived because like…why does the snake make a person and remain in containment? Why does the Foundation let the person the snake made work as part of the Foundation at all let alone be involved in researching the snake? Why does the snake need the Foundation here anyway?

This feels like it really needs you to figure out what makes the snake interesting for a reader to read about, and how it poses challenges to the Foundation, and then from there, to plot out a story of the Foundation interacting with this with like, rising tension and stuff.

Forum thread: The Serpent

item.title: Re: A parallel world
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

the only way to experience and investigate it is through its interaction with two ancient artifacts.

Why do these exist? Like did someone make them and how? More to the point, what does experiencing it and investigating it through them look like? How do they allow this to happen?

Through experimentation and various incidents involving the two artifacts, few things about the parallel world are discovered

My concern with this is that it feels like you're potentially just dumping some information on the reader about this parallel world without giving it weight: the parallel worlds existence should matter for some reason within this narrative so that what it is like is important to a reader; and it feels to me that it's…too emotionally distant? Like the basically complete separation of the parallel world from ours makes it feel to me that it doesn't matter what it's like because like…it can't affect us in any way?

This is not to say that the parallel world has to be dangerous; just that it's existence should have consequences, y'know? It might be that someone accidentally gets trapped there and the Foundation have to get them out; or it could be that stuff from it can affect our world somehow, or something completely different.

And from these consequences, a story should evolve: they should provide tension and allow you to introduce a beginning/middle/end and stuff and like…closure as the consequences are in some way wrapped up, y'know?

item.title: Re: The Mother of a Hell-Spawn Goat Fetus
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

My concern is that a lot of this feels quite reminiscent of SCP-5033 but with a little more of a body horror focus and a much weaker sense of coherency. Iunno, my concern is that everyone within this feels like an unstoppable force: the hunter can do whatever is necessary to kill the SCP and the SCP can never die fully, so there's not a lot of tension here because it's just…inevitable.

Beyond this, there's no real feeling of stakes; you vaguely mention that the fetus wants to revive 'the almighty lucifer' but you say this has been successful and there's really not much of an indication of what that actually like…causes to happen? or why it would matter? or how this revival is tied into the narrative.

I think my advice here would be to focus this more around the hunter than the SCP: I'd likely even swap the two around here and have the hunter be the one in containment; and really focus on his increasingly desperate attempts to get the foundation to let him out so he can hunt the goat; with his powers being very strictly limited to just not dying until he succeeds, y'know?

item.title: Deletions 70: If the fact will not fit the theory – let the theory go.
item.content:encoded:
All Staff-enacted Deletions are carried out according to the Deletions Guide.

Summary deletions result for:

  • Articles with malicious intent
  • Pages that are clearly unfinished.
  • Attempts to "game" site procedure, such as re-posting a non-rewritten article in an attempt to get around downvotes.
  • Blatantly plagiarized material.
  • An article posted outside of the current range.

If an author attempts to self-delete their work and fails to do so properly, including either by blanking the page or renaming it, it will be deleted properly by Staff.
